questions.q: What are the four parts of a Microsoft Purview policy statement?
options: Owner, Reader, Contributor, and Admin
Source, Target, Trigger, and Outcome
Role, Scope, Condition, and Duration
Effect, Action, Data Resource, and Subject
questions.explain: A policy statement is read as a sentence built from exactly these four parts: Effect (Allow), Action (Read/Modify), Data Resource (the asset path), and Subject (who it applies to).

questions.q: What value is currently supported for the Effect field of a policy statement?
options: Only Allow — there is no explicit Deny statement today
Only Deny
Both Allow and Deny, selected from a dropdown
Allow, Deny, and Audit
questions.explain: Today, Effect only supports Allow. Access is opt-in by default: a subject with no matching Allow statement simply has no access.

questions.q: What has to be true on a registered data source before any Purview policy written against it takes effect?
options: Nothing — policies are enforced automatically the moment they're saved
The source has to be deleted and re-registered every time
The source has to be moved to a different Azure region
Data use management has to be switched to Enabled on that source
questions.explain: A source doesn't enforce Purview policies by default. Data use management must be explicitly switched to Enabled on that specific registered source first.

questions.q: Why does publishing a policy require a different Purview role (Data source admin) than writing one (Policy author)?
options: Policy author and Data source admin are actually the same role with two different names
Writing a policy doesn't require any role at all
It's a bug in the Purview portal that Microsoft hasn't fixed yet
It's a deliberate checks-and-balances design — a second set of eyes has to approve before a policy actually goes live
questions.explain: Splitting authoring from publishing means one person can draft a change, but a different person has to review and approve it before it takes effect — preventing a single mistaken or malicious statement from granting access unilaterally.

questions.q: How is a Purview policy different from an Azure RBAC role assignment?
options: A Purview policy can only deny access, never grant it
They are exactly the same system, just with different names
Azure RBAC is only for Purview, and Purview policies are only for Azure Storage
A Purview policy is written and managed inside Purview itself and enforced directly by the registered source, rather than being managed per-resource in the Azure portal
questions.explain: RBAC assignments live in Azure, scoped per resource. A Purview policy lives in Purview, written against a registered source, letting one governance team grant and audit access centrally across many sources instead of it being scattered across Azure subscriptions.
